metadata.remarks: The P0-exit checkpoint promised by r3 and issue #31. Supersedes assessment result 755866ff-18e5-4ca6-aaf1-025eef3ed6e1 (r3, 2026-09-20). Five early-staleness trigger firings are folded in: #37 and #36 on the UUID key grammar, #49 on the trust boundary, #54 on peer verification and deduplication, and #61 recorded as a judgement call. Two findings are added, TM-10 and TM-11, both measured rather than supposed. Identifiers in this record derive under the REGISTERED federation namespace 9f434272-f796-589b-b972-954790395630 (sparc#1155); records before r4 derive under Horizon's placeholder and are left unedited, because an attestation revised in place is not evidence. The expiry is unchanged at 2027-03-18: the 180-day clock runs from the substantive review on 2026-09-19, and resetting it per revision would make a 180-day interval perpetual.

import-ap.remarks: There is no separate assessment plan. The requirement, its scope and its evidencing method are set by docs/dev/issue_rules.md and phase item S0-17 in docs/dev/Implementation_plan.md, which is what this href names. Recorded plainly rather than inventing a plan document to satisfy the field.

results.title: Threat model and security architecture review of the design of record, revision 4 — P0-exit checkpoint
results.description:
Re-review at P0 exit, with the contracts this document reasons about complete: the namespace schema under the registered namespace, the UUIDv5 key grammar and its Go reference, the fixture federation, and API v0 frozen. This is one review of a settled design rather than four of a moving one, which is what the checkpoint cadence was chosen to buy.

Two findings are ADDED. TM-10: two conforming implementations derive different identifiers for one object, with neither side erroring — measured in #54, where every one of the 26 shared vectors agreed and the divergence was in a type rule no vector exercises. TM-11: a trusted OSCAL library drops content and validation passes before AND after, so a pipeline that validates at both ends sees green twice — measured in #49. Neither was reachable by reasoning; both came from running something.

No finding is invalidated. TM-1 gains the refusal semantics settled in #61: an unauthorized node returns 404, indistinguishable from one that does not exist, because a 403 discloses that a boundary exists across organizations not meant to see each other. TM-6 is unchanged and TM-10 sits beside it: TM-6 is a hostile peer exploiting determinism, TM-10 is honest peers disagreeing about what the identifier is.

The inherited-trust table gains two rows it should always have had: the OSCAL type layer, now known to lose content, and SPARC's shared key-grammar contract.

This review also records a process failure. The interim staleness ledger r3 introduced was NOT MAINTAINED: five firings went unlogged for up to two days while the ledger read 'no firing outstanding', and were reconstructed from the git log at this checkpoint — which is the work the ledger exists to avoid. The ledger is now a step-8 obligation in the PR that trips the trigger, and a checkpoint reconstructs from the log regardless rather than trusting an empty table. The failure is recorded rather than quietly corrected, because a mechanism that silently stopped working is what a reader most needs to know about.

observations.title: Threat model re-reviewed and attested at P0 exit, folding in five trigger firings and adding two measured findings
observations.description:
Eleven findings after this review, up from nine. Decisions: one deferred as an open phase-0 decision (TM-4, the chain head has no anchor outside the writer's control), one accepted and inherited (TM-8, deployment), one accepted risk within TM-5, and the rest carried as requirements on the phases that build the affected component — now including TM-10 on P6 with an open cross-repo disagreement (sparc#1175), and TM-11 on P1 and P4.

The checkpoint was due because P0's tasks are complete, not because a phase finished: building what this document requires does not invalidate it, and changing what it assumed does. What changed was the assumptions — the namespace became real, the grammar gained an implementation, and two trusted dependencies turned out to behave differently than assumed.
